| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field), [`page-layout`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#page-layout) |
| In the gallery | [Panels that bleed](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/gallery.html#panels-that-bleed) |
<!-- /facts -->

**A panel can bleed**: its frame runs past the trim, out to the bleed line, and has no border on
that side, so its art goes to the edge of the cut page. `bleed: true` bleeds every side of the
frame that reaches the page's margin; a list bleeds those sides only, and a listed side that does
not reach the margin is a `page-layout` error. The sides are the page's, `top`, `bottom`, `left`
and `right`, whichever way it is read: the page is never mirrored. An inset sits inside its parent,
so it cannot bleed.

![A page whose panels run off its top, left, right and bottom edges, the one beside them bordered all round](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/images/gallery/73-panels-that-bleed.page-1.svg)

A bleeding panel is three boxes. Its **frame** runs to the bleed line: that is its size in its
Core, and what its art, picture, veil and weather cover. What the reader sees stops at the trim, so
its cast is staged and its camera framed in **the frame out to the trim**, and the trim never cuts
a shot. Its lettering keeps inside **the frame as it was** before bleeding, inside the panel margin,
so the page margin stays the safe area for words. Its insets stay where they were. The SVG page is
drawn at its trim, as it will look once cut; its debug view shows the whole sheet, the trim and
each bleeding panel's lettering box.

```yaml
page: {size: [1600, 2400], margin: 80, bleed: 30}
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {wide: {}, look: {}, far: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels: [{use: wide, width: 2, bleed: [top, left]}, {use: look, bleed: true}]
      - panels: [far]
```

**See also:** [`page.bleed`](#pagebleed), the bleed itself.

### `panels[].insets`

<!-- facts: panels[].insets -->
Panels set into its corners, and drawn over it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a list of mappings |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field), [`page-layout`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#page-layout), [`inset-covers-face`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#inset-covers-face) |
| In the gallery | [Insets](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/gallery.html#insets) |
<!-- /facts -->

An **inset** is a small panel set into a corner of another and drawn over it. It sits a gutter in
from both edges of its corner, ringed by a gutter's width of white. The parent is cut around each
inset's ring rather than painted under it, so an inset read first is still on top. The parent's art
is drawn exactly as if the inset were not there; only its lettering moves, since words under an
inset could not be read. When an inset covers a character's face, the compiler notes it.

![A page of five panels outside a cinema, one small panel set into the corner of another](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/images/gallery/26-insets.page-1.svg)

Two insets in one panel must stay a gutter clear of each other, and an inset, a gutter in from its
corner, must fit inside its panel; either is `page-layout` otherwise.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {street: {}, clock: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels:
          - use: street
            insets:
              - {use: clock, at: top_left, size: 0.3}
```

**See also:** [`insets[].read`](#insetsread).

### `columns[].width`

<!-- facts: columns[].width -->
The column's share of its tier's width, relative to the other columns.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0 |
| Default | `1` |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field) |
<!-- /facts -->

A column's share of its tier's width, relative to the other columns, as a panel's `width` is in a
tier of panels.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {above: {}, below: {}, falling: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - columns:
          - {width: 2, panels: [above, below]}
          - {width: 1, panels: [falling]}
```

**See also:** [`tiers[].columns`](#tierscolumns).

### `columns[].panels`

<!-- facts: columns[].panels -->
The panels in the column, read top to bottom.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a list, each text or a mapping |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field) |
<!-- /facts -->

The panels of a column, read top to bottom, each a name or a mapping, as a tier's panels are; a
column holds at least one.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {above: {}, below: {}, falling: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - columns:
          - {panels: [above, {use: below}]}
          - {panels: [falling]}
```

**See also:** [`columns[].panels[].height`](#columnspanelsheight).

### `columns[].panels[].height`

<!-- facts: columns[].panels[].height -->
The panel's share of its column's height, relative to the others in it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0 |
| Default | `1` |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field) |
<!-- /facts -->

A panel's share of its column's height, relative to the others in it.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {above: {}, below: {}, falling: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - columns:
          - {panels: [above, {use: below, height: 2}]}
          - {panels: [falling]}
```

**See also:** [`tiers[].height`](#tiersheight).

### `insets[].use`

<!-- facts: insets[].use -->
The name of a panel under `panels:`, set into this one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | text |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field), [`page-layout`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#page-layout) |
<!-- /facts -->

The panel set into the corner, by its name under `panels:`. Like any panel on a page, it is placed
once.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {street: {}, face: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels: [{use: street, insets: [{use: face, at: bottom_right, size: 0.3}]}]
```

**See also:** [`panels[].insets`](#panelsinsets).

### `insets[].at`

<!-- facts: insets[].at -->
The corner of its parent the inset sits in, a gutter in from both edges.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `top_left`, `top_right`, `bottom_left`, `bottom_right` |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field), [`inset-covers-face`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#inset-covers-face) |
<!-- /facts -->

The corner of its parent. The corner is the parent's whichever way the page is read: an inset's
`at` is never mirrored.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {street: {}, clock: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels: [{use: street, insets: [{use: clock, at: top_right, size: 0.25}]}]
```

**See also:** [`insets[].size`](#insetssize).

### `insets[].size`

<!-- facts: insets[].size -->
The inset's width and height, as a fraction of its parent's: above 0, at most 0.5.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0, at most 0.5 |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field), [`page-layout`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#page-layout), [`inset-covers-face`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#inset-covers-face) |
<!-- /facts -->

The inset's width and height, as one fraction of its parent's: `0.25` is a quarter as wide and a
quarter as tall. More than half would leave the parent covered rather than inset.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {street: {}, clock: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels: [{use: street, insets: [{use: clock, at: top_left, size: 0.45}]}]
```

**See also:** [`insets[].at`](#insetsat).

### `insets[].read`

<!-- facts: insets[].read -->
When the inset is read: `after` its parent, or `before` it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A `.scene.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `before`, `after` |
| Default | `after` |
| Since | 0.10 |
| Diagnostics | [`invalid-field`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#invalid-field) |
<!-- /facts -->

Readers split about evenly over whether an inset comes before the panel it sits in or after it
(Cohn, 2013), so it is never guessed: an inset is read right after its parent unless it says
`read: before`. That is the order the page's SVG writes them in, which is the order a screen reader
follows.

```yaml
cast: {alice: {reference: alice}}
panels: {street: {}, clock: {}}
pages:
  - tiers:
      - panels: [{use: street, insets: [{use: clock, at: top_left, size: 0.25, read: before}]}]
```

**See also:** the reading order of a page, [`pages`](#pages).

### Read right to left

With [`direction: rtl`](#direction), the same page is read from the top right. Panels
are still written in reading order, so the first panel of a tier is at its right and the last at its
left; the first column of a tier of columns is at the right, and each column is still read top to
bottom -- a stack beside a tall panel is read down before across, on the right. Each frame is
exactly the one a left-to-right page gives that panel with the tier written the other way round, so
every panel keeps its size, and its art is the art it has read left to right. What names a place on
the page keeps naming it: an inset's `at:` is a corner of its parent, a positive `slant` leans the
top of each gutter right, as written, and a `bleed` names the page's own sides, so `bleed: [left]`
on a tier's first panel, which right to left is at the right, is refused. Any other layout one
direction refuses, the other refuses too.

## Puppet files

A puppet of your own is a `*.puppet.yaml` file: a skeleton in its own units, the parts
drawn on it, the landmarks a shot crops at, a face, and the poses and expressions it can take, by
name. A [cast member](#castidreference) names it by its path, relative to the document, and
the compiler reads only what that cast names. What the solver sees of it, and why, is in the
[asset contract](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/asset_contract.html#skeletal-puppets); this page has a card for every key.

Every fault in a puppet file is `puppet-file`: at the key that is wrong, in the puppet file, when the
document naming it is checked as a file, and on the line naming it otherwise. Its schema is
`scenet schema --puppet`, which an editor associates with `*.puppet.yaml`; what no schema can say --
landmarks increasing downward, a skeleton that is a tree, every joint a part or a pose names
declared -- `scenet check` does.

### A puppet file

Every card below points here. This is Pip, the gallery's puppet, five heads tall; the panel after it
casts Pip beside Alice.

*puppets/pip.puppet.yaml:*

```yaml
# Pip: a child, five heads tall, and the gallery's own puppet -- Scenet does not ship it.
#
# A document casts it by its path, relative to the document, as it names a font or a
# picture: `reference: puppets/pip.puppet.yaml`. The `name:` below is what a message calls it.
#
# What sets it apart from alice and bob, who are both seven and a half heads tall:
#
# - Five heads, not seven and a half. A head is the same 100 units as alice's, so the body
#   below it is shorter, and the head is big for it -- a child's proportion. At the same
#   shot, a camera that framed by fractions of the panel instead of by landmarks in heads
#   would get pip visibly wrong.
# - Big eyes, set low in the face, a small nose and a small mouth.
# - A knot of hair on top of the head: a blob, as the head is, so pip reads as pip even at
#   a distance, where a face is too small to draw.
#
# Values are native units, one head being 100; landmarks are measured down from the top of
# the head, and each joint's offset from its parent's. The root sits at the waist.

name: pip
units_per_head: 100
root: root
root_landmark: waist

landmarks:
  head_top: 0
  eyes: 50
  chin: 100
  shoulders: 120
  chest: 165
  waist: 245
  mid_thigh: 320
  knees: 375
  feet: 500

joints:
  root: {parent: null, offset: [0, 0]}
  spine: {parent: root, offset: [0, -80]}
  neck: {parent: spine, offset: [0, -45]}
  head: {parent: neck, offset: [0, -70]}

  shoulder_l: {parent: neck, offset: [-26, 4]}
  shoulder_r: {parent: neck, offset: [26, 4]}
  elbow_l: {parent: shoulder_l, offset: [0, 62]}
  elbow_r: {parent: shoulder_r, offset: [0, 62]}
  wrist_l: {parent: elbow_l, offset: [0, 55]}
  wrist_r: {parent: elbow_r, offset: [0, 55]}

  hip_l: {parent: root, offset: [-20, 8]}
  hip_r: {parent: root, offset: [20, 8]}
  knee_l: {parent: hip_l, offset: [0, 122]}
  knee_r: {parent: hip_r, offset: [0, 122]}
  ankle_l: {parent: knee_l, offset: [0, 125]}
  ankle_r: {parent: knee_r, offset: [0, 125]}

parts:
  - {from: neck, to: root, width: 64}
  - {from: shoulder_l, to: elbow_l, width: 22}
  - {from: elbow_l, to: wrist_l, width: 18}
  - {from: shoulder_r, to: elbow_r, width: 22}
  - {from: elbow_r, to: wrist_r, width: 18}
  - {from: hip_l, to: knee_l, width: 28}
  - {from: knee_l, to: ankle_l, width: 24}
  - {from: hip_r, to: knee_r, width: 28}
  - {from: knee_r, to: ankle_r, width: 24}
  - {at: head, radius: 50}
  - {at: head, radius: 16, offset: [0, -56]}   # the knot of hair

anchors:
  head_top: {joint: head, offset: [0, -50]}
  eyes: {joint: head, offset: [0, 0]}
  mouth: {joint: head, offset: [0, 26]}
  feet: {joint: root, offset: [0, 255]}

face:
  joint: head
  radius: 60
  # Feature points ride the head joint, so they mirror and scale with it. `size` means an
  # eye's radius, a brow's or mouth's half-width, a nose's length.
  features:
    brow_l: {offset: [-19, -22], size: 10}
    brow_r: {offset: [19, -22], size: 10}
    eye_l:  {offset: [-19, -2], size: 12}
    eye_r:  {offset: [19, -2], size: 12}
    nose:   {offset: [0, 12], size: 6}
    mouth:  {offset: [0, 26], size: 12}

gaze:
  origin: eyes

poses:
  standing_neutral:
    elbow_l: -5
    elbow_r: 5

  waving:
    elbow_l: -5
    elbow_r: -150
    wrist_r: 35

  arms_up:
    elbow_l: 155
    wrist_l: -20
    elbow_r: -155
    wrist_r: 20

expressions:
  neutral:  {}
  happy:    {mouth: smile}
  surprise: {brow: raised,     eyes: wide, mouth: open}
  scared:   {brow: angled_out, eyes: wide, mouth: small}
  sad:      {brow: angled_out, eyes: half, mouth: frown}
```

```yaml
camera: {shot: full_shot}
cast:
  alice: {reference: alice, at: left_third}
  pip: {reference: puppets/pip.puppet.yaml, pose: arms_up, expression: happy, at: right_third, facing: left}
staging: [alice ground_shared_with pip]
```

### `name`

<!-- facts: name -->
The name a cast member's `reference` uses.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | text |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The name the puppet goes by in messages and in Panel Core. A cast member names a puppet file by its
path, not by this, so two files may share a name without either shadowing the other or a shipped
puppet. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `units_per_head`

<!-- facts: units_per_head -->
How many of the puppet's own units one head height is.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0 |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The puppet's own unit, against the one measure every shot is defined in: a head height. Offsets,
widths and radii are in the puppet's units; landmarks are in heads. A figure is as tall as its
`feet` landmark says, in heads -- Pip is five, Alice seven and a half. See
[the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `landmarks`

<!-- facts: landmarks -->
Each vertical body landmark, as a distance down from the top of the head, in head units: the crop lines a shot type names.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The nine crop lines a shot names, each as a distance down from the top of the head, in heads:
`head_top`, `eyes`, `chin`, `shoulders`, `chest`, `waist`, `mid_thigh`, `knees` and `feet`. All nine
are required, because any shot may crop at any of them, and they must increase downward. What each
shot does with them is in [Shot types](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/shot_types.html). See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `landmarks.head_top`

<!-- facts: landmarks.head_top -->
The origin every other landmark is measured down from.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | `0` |
| Values | `0` |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The origin every other landmark is measured down from, so it is `0`. See
[the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `joints`

<!-- facts: joints -->
The skeleton, by joint name.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The skeleton, by joint name: a tree rooted at [`root`](#root), every joint reaching it through its
parents. A joint's pose angle rotates the bone arriving at it *and* everything below it, which is
what makes posing read naturally: bending `elbow_l` swings the forearm and takes the hand with it.
See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `joints.<joint>.parent`

<!-- facts: joints.<joint>.parent -->
The joint it hangs from. Left out for the root.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | text |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The joint this one hangs from. The root has none, and every other joint must reach the root: a
cycle, or a joint that hangs from nothing, is refused. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `joints.<joint>.offset`

<!-- facts: joints.<joint>.offset -->
Where it is from its parent in the rest pose, in the puppet's own units.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | `[number, number]` |
| Default | `[0, 0]` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

Where the joint is from its parent in the rest pose, `[x, y]` in the puppet's units, with y
downward. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `root`

<!-- facts: root -->
The joint every other one hangs from.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | text |
| Default | `root` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The joint every other one hangs from. It must be declared, with no parent. See
[the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `root_landmark`

<!-- facts: root_landmark -->
The landmark the root joint sits at.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `head_top`, `eyes`, `chin`, `shoulders`, `chest`, `waist`, `mid_thigh`, `knees`, `feet` |
| Default | `waist` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The landmark the root joint physically sits at. The skeleton is built outward from the root, while
landmarks are measured downward from the top of the head; this is what bridges the two frames.
Declared rather than assumed, because a puppet may root itself somewhere other than the waist. See
[the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `parts`

<!-- facts: parts -->
The shapes the body is drawn from, back to front.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a list of mappings |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

What is drawn, back to front: each part a **bone**, a capsule between two joints, or a **blob**, a
disc at one. A part's keys say which kind it is: `from` and `to` make a bone, `at` makes a blob. A
part is checked only as the kind it is written as, and one that uses the keys of both kinds, or of
neither, is a single error saying so. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

<!-- facts: anchors -->
Named attachment points, such as `mouth` and `eyes`, each on a joint.

### `face`

<!-- facts: face -->
Where the face is, and what is drawn in it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

The disc no balloon, caption or sound effect may cover, and what is drawn inside it. A circle rather
than a polygon: faces are roughly round, the test is cheap, and a slightly generous face only puts a

<!-- facts: face.radius -->
The face's radius, in the puppet's own units: the circle no balloon covers.

| | |
|---|---|

| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0 |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

[the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `face.features`

<!-- facts: face.features -->
What is drawn inside the face, by feature. Empty for a plain round head.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

What is drawn inside the face, by feature: `brow_l`, `brow_r`, `eye_l`, `eye_r`, `nose` and
`mouth`, named after MPEG-4's facial feature groups. Each is optional -- a stylised character may
have no eyebrows -- but a pair comes in pairs, since a face with one eyebrow is a typo far more often
than it is a character. Pupils are not declared: they are placed inside each eye toward whoever the
character is looking at. A puppet with no features is drawn as it was before faces existed, a
filled circle, and may declare no expressions. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

[the example](#a-puppet-file).

[the example](#a-puppet-file).

<!-- facts: face.features.<feature>.size -->
How big the feature is drawn, in the puppet's own units: an eye's radius, a brow's or a mouth's half-width, a nose's length.

| | |
|---|---|

What the number means depends on the feature: an eye's radius, a brow's or a mouth's half-width, a

### `poses`

<!-- facts: poses -->
Named poses, each a set of joint angles.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

Named poses, each a mapping of joint to angle, in degrees, that a cast member selects with
[`pose`](#castidpose). A joint a pose leaves out keeps its rest angle. `standing_neutral` is
required of every puppet, since it is what a member gets when it names no pose, and every joint a
pose names must be declared. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `expressions`

<!-- facts: expressions -->
Named expressions, each a state of brow, eyes and mouth.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

Named expressions, each a state of the brows, the eyes and the mouth, that a cast member selects
with [`expression`](#castidexpression). An expression is to features what a pose is to
joints, but a face deforms rather than rotating about bones, which is why it is a set of states and
not of angles. A puppet that declares any declares `neutral`, which a member gets unasked, and has
face features for them to move. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `expressions.<expression>.brow`

<!-- facts: expressions.<expression>.brow -->
The brows' state.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `neutral`, `raised`, `lowered`, `angled_in`, `angled_out` |
| Default | `neutral` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

What the eyebrows are doing. `angled_in` puts the inner ends down, the anger brow; `angled_out` puts
them up, the sad or frightened one. Inner and outer are taken against the face's centre rather than
the page, so both survive mirroring. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `expressions.<expression>.eyes`

<!-- facts: expressions.<expression>.eyes -->
The eyes' state.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `open`, `wide`, `narrowed`, `half`, `closed` |
| Default | `open` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

How open the eyes are. `half` is the heavy-lidded eye of boredom, distinct from `narrowed`, the
squint of anger or suspicion: one droops, the other is tightened. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

### `expressions.<expression>.mouth`

<!-- facts: expressions.<expression>.mouth -->
The mouth's state.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | A puppet file, a `.puppet.yaml`. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a name |
| Values | `neutral`, `flat`, `smile`, `grin`, `frown`, `open`, `small` |
| Default | `neutral` |
| Since | 0.13 |
| Diagnostics | [`puppet-file`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#puppet-file) |
<!-- /facts -->

What the mouth is doing. `grin` is an open smile, `smile` a closed one, and `small` the reticent
little mouth that does most of the work in a coy face. See [the example](#a-puppet-file).

## Artwork contracts

A supplied picture can draw its own people. Where each face, mouth and body is, the panel never
says -- it never writes a coordinate. The picture's **artwork contract** does: a file beside the
picture, named after it, `art/p01-street.art.yaml` beside `art/p01-street.png`, measured once in
the picture's own pixels and committed with it. A cast member names a figure it declares with
[`figure:`](#castidfigure). What the solver does with it is in the
[asset contract](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/asset_contract.html#artwork-contracts); this page has a card for every key.

The contract is read only for a panel whose cast names a figure, and its geometry goes through the
picture's [`fit`](#settingfit), so a face is excluded exactly where the picture draws it,
under `cover` and `contain` alike. `scenet check` reads it without running the solver, and reports a
missing or malformed one as `artwork-contract`: in the contract itself, at the line of the fault,
when the document is checked as a file; at the line naming the picture when it is checked as text,
as in the playground or over MCP. `scenet build --debug` draws every face, mouth, body and keep-out
over the panel, which is how a contract is checked against its picture.

### An artwork contract

Every card below points here: the gallery's contract for `art/figures.png`, a station platform at
night with three people on it, and a panel that casts two of them.

*art/figures.art.yaml:*

```yaml
# The artwork contract for figures.png, written by scripts/make_gallery_figures.py
# from the same constants the picture is painted from. Pixels, from the top left.
size: [900, 600]
figures:
  ana:
    face: {center: [230, 250], radius: 56}
    mouth: [230, 273]
    body: [[168, 296], [292, 296], [316, 600], [144, 600]]
  ben:
    face: {center: [410, 236], radius: 60}
    mouth: [410, 261]
    body: [[340, 286], [480, 286], [502, 600], [318, 600]]
  carl:
    face: {center: [720, 300], radius: 46}
    mouth: [720, 319]
    body: [[668, 338], [772, 338], [786, 600], [654, 600]]
keep_out:
  # The timetable board.
  - [[560, 60], [860, 60], [860, 200], [560, 200]]
```

```yaml
panel: {size: [900, 600]}
setting: {image: art/figures.png, time: night}
cast:
  ana: {figure: ana}
  ben: {figure: ben}
script:
  - say: {by: ana, text: "Is that ours?"}
  - say: {by: ben, text: "No."}
```

### `size`

<!-- facts: size -->
The picture's size in pixels, `[width, height]`, as it was measured. It must be the picture's own.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | `[number, number]` |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

The picture's size in pixels, as the contract was measured against it. It must be the picture's
own: a contract measured on another size of the picture would put every face somewhere else, so a
mismatch is refused rather than scaled. See [the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures`

<!-- facts: figures -->
Each figure the picture draws, by the name a cast member's `figure` gives it. Every face here is kept clear of lettering, cast or not.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

**Everybody the contract declares is in the picture.** A face nobody cast is as forbidden to
lettering as a speaker's, and a body as costly to cover: a crowd of five can be declared and two of
them cast. A figure a panel casts and the contract does not declare is `unknown-figure`, listing
the ones it does. See [the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures.<name>.face`

<!-- facts: figures.<name>.face -->
The figure's face: a disc no balloon, caption or sound effect may cover.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a mapping |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

The face, as a disc. A contract declares no gaze, so nothing keeps a balloon out of a figure's line
of sight; the face is all lettering keeps clear of. See [the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures.<name>.face.center`

<!-- facts: figures.<name>.face.center -->
The face's centre, `[x, y]` in the picture's pixels, from its top left.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | `[number, number]` |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

The face's centre, in pixels from the picture's top left; it must lie on the picture. See
[the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures.<name>.face.radius`

<!-- facts: figures.<name>.face.radius -->
How far the face reaches, in pixels. Generous is safer than tight: no lettering overlaps this disc, and a tail stops on its edge.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a number |
| Values | above 0 |
| Default | none: required |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

Generous is safer than tight: no balloon may overlap the disc at all, and a tail stops on its edge.
A `cover` crop that pushes part of a face out of the panel keeps clear whatever part is in view. See
[the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures.<name>.mouth`

<!-- facts: figures.<name>.mouth -->
Where the tail of a line the figure speaks ends, or the place a sound it makes comes from, in pixels. Left out, a tail aims at the face's centre.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | `[number, number]` |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

Where a tail ends, and where a sound the figure makes comes from. A tail to a mouth that a `cover`
crop cuts away ends on the frame, aimed at it, and `scenet build` says so in a note. See
[the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `figures.<name>.body`

<!-- facts: figures.<name>.body -->
The figure's silhouette, a polygon in pixels, which a balloon pays to cover: half as much over its own speaker.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a list of `[number, number]` |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

A polygon of at least three points, in pixels, simple -- no edge crossing another. Covering a
figure's body costs a balloon, and covering its own speaker's costs half, as with a puppet. See
[the example](#an-artwork-contract).

### `keep_out`

<!-- facts: keep_out -->
Regions lettering should stay off, each a polygon in pixels: a sign, a hand, what the panel is about. A cost, not a rule.

| | |
|---|---|
| Where | An artwork contract, the `.art.yaml` beside its picture. Not in a comic script |
| Type | a list of a list of `[number, number]` |
| Default | none |
| Since | 0.12 |
| Diagnostics | [`artwork-contract`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/diagnostics.html#artwork-contract) |
<!-- /facts -->

**Keep-out regions** are ground lettering pays to cover, weighted as emanata are -- a sign, a hand,
what the panel is about -- and never forbidden: a crowded panel covers one before it fails. Each is
a simple polygon on the picture. See [the example](#an-artwork-contract).

<!-- scenet-spec:part=shot-types -->
# Shot types (normative)

How the camera's `shot` value determines the scale of a figure in the panel.

## The unit: head-heights

Figures are measured in **head-heights**, the standard figure-drawing unit. An adult is
conventionally about 7.5 heads tall. Every puppet declares `units_per_head` and a set of vertical
**landmarks** measured downward from `head_top`, so the compiler can reason about anatomy without
knowing anything about the artwork.

## Why not "60% of panel height"

A tempting shortcut is to define each shot as a fixed fraction of panel height. It is wrong, because
what a shot type actually names is **where the frame cuts the body** — the waist, the chest, the
shoulders. The fraction of the panel that a figure then occupies falls out of that crop, and differs
between a child and an adult, or between a standing and a seated pose. Encoding the fraction instead
of the crop line bakes in one body and one pose.

So a shot type is defined by two things: a **crop landmark**, and a **headroom** fraction — the empty
space above the head that stops the figure colliding with the top edge.

## Resolution

```
visible_height_native = landmark[crop].y - landmark[head_top].y
available_height      = panel_height * (1 - headroom - footroom)
scale                 = available_height / visible_height_native
```

The scaled figure is then anchored so its crop line meets the bottom of the available area.
`footroom` is the shot's own, from the [table](#table): `0.0` unless the shot lists one. No key
sets it; a panel chooses it by choosing the shot.

This anchoring rule is right whenever the crop landmark sits at the **edge** of what the shot
frames -- feet at the bottom of a long shot, chin at the bottom of a big close-up. It goes wrong at
the one rung where the landmark sits **inside** the thing being framed: `extreme_close_up` crops at
`eyes`, and bottom-anchoring the eyes puts the whole eye region below the panel, framing forehead
and eyebrows instead. Headroom cannot fix this -- it shifts the figure down and shrinks it by
exactly the same amount, so the crop line stays pinned to `panel_height * (1 - footroom)`
regardless of headroom. Footroom is the only lever that moves a crop line up from the bottom edge,
which is why `extreme_close_up` is the one shot in the table that needs it despite showing no feet.

## Table

A comic script may name these in French; see
[French scripts](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/howto/write_a_comic_script.html#french-scripts) for the rung-by-rung table.

| `shot` | Crop landmark | Headroom | Footroom | Reads as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `long_shot` (alias `wide`) | `feet` | 0.28 | 0.10 | Figure small in its environment |
| `full_shot` | `feet` | 0.05 | 0.04 | Whole body, environment secondary |
| `medium_full` | `knees` | 0.08 | — | The three-quarter shot |
| `cowboy` | `mid_thigh` | 0.08 | — | Stance and confrontation |
| `medium_shot` | `waist` | 0.10 | — | The conversational default |
| `medium_close_up` | `chest` | 0.10 | — | Emphasis on the speaker |
| `close_up` | `shoulders` | 0.08 | — | Emotion; face dominates |
| `big_close_up` | `chin` | 0.05 | — | Intensity |
| `extreme_close_up` | `eyes` | 0.00 | 0.45 | Crops through the face deliberately |

**`wide` is an exact synonym for `long_shot`.** The two are used interchangeably in the
literature and the language keeps both because writers reach for both.

**`medium_full` and `cowboy` are not synonyms**, though they were briefly implemented as
though they were. Medium full — the three-quarter shot — cuts at the knees. The cowboy
or American shot cuts at mid-thigh, a framing that comes from 1930s Westerns needing the
holster in shot. Naming two shots and drawing one collapses a rung of the ladder, and
nothing about the output makes that visible.

**Footroom is space left below the crop line.** For the two shots that show feet, that space
reads as ground, and it is not decoration. The crop lands the `feet` *landmark* on the frame
edge, but the drawing continues past it: the ankle joint sits exactly on that landmark and the
shin is drawn as a round-capped stroke, so half its width falls below. Without footroom a long
shot clipped the feet by nine panel units — the one thing a long shot is defined by not doing.
It is also compositionally right on its own: a figure standing on the exact bottom edge reads
as falling out of the panel rather than standing on anything.

`extreme_close_up` uses footroom for a different reason: its crop landmark (`eyes`) is inside
the face rather than at its edge, and footroom is the only lever that moves a crop line up off
the bottom edge — see **Resolution**, above.

The table is **monotonic**: reading down it, the figure never gets smaller. That is what
makes it a ladder, and it is enforced by a test rather than left to inspection —
`long_shot` and `full_shot` crop at the same landmark, so only headroom separates them,
and having those two the wrong way round inverted the ladder at its widest end without
anything noticing.

**`long_shot` and `full_shot` crop at the same landmark**, so headroom and footroom are all
that separate them. Until the [setting layer](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/setting.html#setting) existed the gap between them
had to stay modest: with nothing behind the figure, air is just white, and a small figure alone on
a page reads as a full shot with a generous margin rather than as a long shot. Now the air is the
environment — which is what a long shot is *about* — so the gap is a real rung, and a long shot
frames the figure at roughly two thirds the size a full shot does. The environment may be masses or
a [supplied picture](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/setting.html#settingimage): the camera reads neither, so a shot
frames the cast the same in front of either.

## Angle

`angle` scales the shot's **headroom**, the air above the head. That is the cue a reader takes
from an angle, and it is one that survives being drawn flat:

| `angle` | Headroom | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `low` | × 0.5 | Less air above the head: the figure looms; viewer looks up |
| `eye_level` | × 1.0 | The shot's own headroom (default) |
| `high` | × 1.6 | More air above: the figure is diminished; viewer looks down |

A tilted camera never leaves less than 0.02 of the panel height above the head, so a shot whose
own headroom is zero, such as `extreme_close_up`, still moves under an angle.

**Current limitation:** angle changes headroom only. It does not apply perspective projection or
foreshortening, because the compiler is orthographic, so an extreme angle reads as the figure
sitting higher or lower rather than as a change of viewpoint. This is a known gap, not an
oversight.

<!-- scenet-spec:part=comic-script -->
# Write a panel as a comic script

Comic writers already have a format. It is not YAML, it has been in use for decades, and
asking someone to abandon it in order to try a compiler is a poor trade.

So Scenet reads it.

*umbrella.script:*

```scenet-script
---
cast:
  ALICE: {reference: alice, at: left_third}
  BOB:   {reference: bob,   at: right_third, facing: left}
---

PAGE ONE

PANEL 1
@shot: full_shot
CAPTION: Midnight. The docks.
Alice and Bob face each other on a rainy street corner. She is exasperated.

ALICE
You forgot your umbrella!

BOB
I know.

PANEL 2
@shot: medium_close_up
Closer now. Bob will not meet her eye.

BOB (whisper)
I left it on purpose.

ALICE (shouting)
You what?!
```

The lines between the `---` fences are the [front matter](#front-matter): who `ALICE` and `BOB`
are, which a script has no way to say. Everything under them is the script as a writer writes it.
Save that as `umbrella.script` and compile it exactly like any other document:

```bash
scenet build umbrella.script --strip
```

The gallery's `examples/gallery/13-comic-script.script` is a script like it:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=13-comic-script.script).
Each convention below has an example of its own there, written the way writers who use it write.

## The rules

| Line | Means |
|---|---|
| `PANEL 1` | Starts a new panel. `PANEL 1:`, `PANEL 1.` and `Panel One` are the same panel. |
| `Panel 1. Alice and Bob on a corner.` | Dark Horse's form: the panel, and its description on the same line. |
| `@shot: full_shot` | A directive. `@shot` and `@angle` set the camera; anything else sets a top-level panel key. Each is written once per panel: a second is reported, not quietly kept. |
| `ALICE` (all caps, alone) | The lines after it, up to a blank line, are one speech by `ALICE`. |
| `BOB (small)` | Muttered: smaller type, in a balloon that keeps its room. `(weak)` is the same. |
| `BOB (whisper)` | Same, with a balloon kind: `(whisper)` or `(whispering)`, `(shout)`, `(shouting)`, `(yell)` or `(yelling)`, `(thought)` or `(thinking)`. `(burst)` is a shout. Several parentheticals, or one with commas, are read together. |
| `ALICE: Hello.` | A cue with its line on the same line. Dialogue when `ALICE` is in the panel's cast; see below. |
| `ALICE (V.O.)` | A voice over: the line is a spoken caption by `ALICE`, not a balloon. `(VO)` and `(VOICE OVER)` too. |
| `ALICE (OP)` | Dark Horse's off-panel speech: Alice is left out of this panel, and her balloon's tail ends on the frame. `(OFF)`, `(off-panel)`, `(O.S.)` and `(O.C.)` too. |
| `ALICE (OP, left)` | Same, from the side named: `left`, `right`, `top` or `bottom`. A side alone is a note for the artist. |
| `CAPTION: Midnight.`, `CAP: Midnight.` | A caption box, its text on the same line. |
| `CAP:` or `CAPTION` (alone) | Dark Horse's form: the caption's text is on the lines under it, to a blank line. |
| `CAPTION (monologue): ...` | Same, with a caption kind: `(locale)`, `(monologue)`, `(spoken)` or `(editorial)`. `(voice over)` is the spoken kind. |
| `CAP/ALICE` | Dark Horse's caption carrying a character's speech: a spoken caption by `ALICE`. |
| `1. ALICE:`, `2) CAP:` | Blambot's numbered lettering items: the number is set aside. |
| `SFX: BLAM` | A sound effect. The sound is on the same line. |
| `SFX (BOB, large): KRAK` | Same, coming from `BOB`, at a size. |
| `SFX:` (alone) | Dark Horse's form: the sound is on the next line. |
| Anything else | Prose. Preserved, never interpreted. |
| `PAGE ONE` | Starts a page: the panels under it are laid out on it. See [Pages](#pages). |
| `PAGE ONE (five panels)` | Dark Horse's form: the page, and how many panels it has. A count its panels do not match is a `panel-count` note. |
| `@tiers: 2 1 2` | Right after a PAGE heading: how many panels each tier of that page holds, from the top. |
| `## PANEL 2`, `**PANEL 2**`, `---` | Markdown: the markers are stripped and the heading read; a horizontal rule is a blank line. |
| Before the first heading | The title page: the writer's name and address, the title. Kept, never interpreted. |

The one detail that trips people up: **a speaker cue is recognised by the name being all
caps, not the whole line.** `BOB (whisper)` qualifies, because only `BOB` is tested. Capitals
with accents are capitals: `HÉLÈNE` and `ZOË` are cues. The script is read composed (Unicode
NFC), so a name your editor stored as a letter and a separate accent is the same name the
front matter spells, and a byte-order mark at the start of the file is ignored.

**A speech runs until a blank line.** Wrap a long line of dialogue wherever you like; the lines
are joined with a space into one balloon. A line that looks like another cue ends the speech
and starts the next, so two speeches need no blank line between them.

**Underline a word by writing it between underscores**: `I _told_ you.` Scripts underline the
words to stress, and a letterer sets them in bold italic, which is what the compiler does — in
dialogue and in captions alike. The rules are in
[the language reference](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/script.html#saytext).

**Panel numbers may start again on each page**, as publishers' script formats ask. When they
do, every panel is named by its page as well: `PANEL 1` under `PAGE TWO` is panel `2-1`, and
`scenet build` writes it to `name.2-1.svg`. A page spelled out in English is named by its
number (`PAGE TWO` is page `2`, `PAGE TWENTY-ONE` page `21`); anything else is kept as written
(`PAGE 3A`). A script that numbers its panels straight through keeps the plain names. Two
panels that would still share a name, such as `PANEL 1` twice on one page, are reported as
`duplicate-panel` rather than one quietly replacing the other.

**A sound effect is an `SFX` line**, written where it happens in the script, as publishers ask
for everything to be listed in reading order. The parenthetical says who or what it comes from — a
name from the cast — and how loud, `small`, `medium` or `large`, in either order. Dark Horse writes
`SFX:` as a cue with the sound under it; that works too, and the line under it is the sound however
it looks — `BLAM` is in capitals, which would otherwise make it a character's cue. An `SFX:` cue with
nothing under it is reported rather than dropped. Turns, arcs and hollow letters are written in YAML;
see [`sfx`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/script.html#sfx).

`CAP`, `CAPTION` and `SFX` are checked before speaker cues, because as far as the cue pattern
is concerned each is a perfectly good character name. So they are reserved: none can be a cast
member's id. A caption or a sound effect with its text to follow also wins over a cue waiting for
its line — `BOB (whisper)` then `CAPTION: Later.` is a caption, and a note says Bob had nothing
to say.

**A cue may carry its line after a colon**, `ALICE: Hello.`, as Dark Horse's guide itself does. A
writer's note to the artist looks exactly the same — `NOTE: redraw the rain` — so the line is
dialogue only when the name is in the panel's cast: the front matter's, and any `@cast:` in the
panel, wherever in it. A name in capitals that is not in the cast is read as it would otherwise
be — prose, or a wrapped line of the speech above — and a `looks-like-dialogue` note says so, since
a misspelled speaker looks the same. A name in lower case, `Junior: Die, you dirty rat!`, is
dialogue only when it is exactly a cast member's id, and otherwise silent prose.

**A caption can carry speech.** Dark Horse's `CAP/ALICE`, with the words in quotation marks,
is a `spoken` caption by `ALICE`. The compiler letters a spoken caption's quotation marks itself
— one opening each box, one closing the speaker's last — so the writer's are taken off rather
than doubled, and so is one enclosing pair around a balloon's text. A voice over, `ALICE (V.O.)`,
is the same thing written as a cue: [Blambot](https://blambot.com/pages/comic-script-basics)
defines `CAPTION (VOICE OVER)` as a character "speaking, but … not in the location shown".

## A script as publishers ask for it

[Dark Horse's script format](https://images.darkhorse.com/darkhorse08/company/submissions/DHScriptFormatGuides.pdf)
is the reference house format, and Scenet reads its layout as written:

*Part of a script in Dark Horse's format, less its front matter:*

```scenet-script
Margo Wren
14 Harbour Lane, Port Ellis

PAGE ONE (two panels)

Panel 1. A lighthouse on a cliff at dusk. Maya climbs the last of the steps.

MAYA:
Theo? The lamp is out --

Panel 2. Inside. Theo kneels by the dead lamp.

THEO (whisper):
-- because somebody forgot the oil.
```

- **The title page** is everything before the first heading. It is kept and never read,
  as prose is. A name in capitals with a line under it looks like a cue, so it is pointed
  out as a `looks-like-dialogue` note; a name from the cast there is an error, since it is
  far more likely a missing PANEL heading. A directive, a caption or a sound effect before
  the first heading belongs to no panel, and is an error.
- **A line between a PAGE heading and its first PANEL** belongs to the page, never to the
  last panel of the page before, which is where it used to end up.
- **`PAGE ONE (five panels)`** states the count. When the panels under it number something
  else, a heading has usually been missed, so it is a `panel-count` note. Any other
  parenthetical, `(splash)` say, is a note to the artist, and is not read as a count.
- **`Panel 1.` with its description on the same line** is a heading when the label looks
  like a number — digits, digits and a letter, one letter, or a number in words — so
  that `Panel shows Alice.` stays the sentence it is.
- **`--`**, Dark Horse's mark for a speech carried to the next balloon, is kept as written,
  and is never set at the start of a line or alone on one.
- **A cue with nothing said under it** is a `looks-like-dialogue` note rather than vanishing.

`examples/gallery/31-dark-horse.script` is a script in this format, title page and all:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=31-dark-horse.script).

## A script kept in Markdown

Writers keep scripts in Markdown, so `#` to `######` before a heading, `**` or `__` around
it or around a label, and a horizontal rule are tolerated: the markers are stripped and the
convention read. It is not a second format: the text of a line is never rewritten.

*Part of a comic script kept in Markdown:*

```scenet-script
## PAGE ONE

### PANEL 2
**Alice** waits on the corner, soaked.

**alice:** You forgot your _umbrella_.

---

**PANEL 3**
```

- **A rule, `---`, `***` or `___`, is a blank line**, and parts two panels as one does.
- **A name in lower case is a cue when it is a cast id**, written with its line after the
  colon: `alice:` speaks when the front matter casts `alice`, as a YAML panel would. Alone on
  its line, a name is a cue only in capitals.
- **A word between underscores is stressed**, in the lettering. In prose, Markdown's markers
  round a word are taken off the description a screen reader is given.

`examples/gallery/63-a-markdown-script.script` is a script kept this way, with a cover panel
before its first PAGE heading:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=63-a-markdown-script.script).

## A letterer's script

[Blambot's comic script basics](https://blambot.com/pages/comic-script-basics) asks writers
to number every item a letterer letters, in reading order, and to say what each is. Scenet
reads it so:

- **`1.`, `2)` before a label** is a lettering item's number, and is set aside.
- **A caption's kind in parentheses**: `(locale)`, `(monologue)`, `(spoken)`, `(editorial)`,
  and Blambot's `CAPTION (VOICE OVER)`, which is the spoken kind.
- **A balloon's kind**: `(OFF)` from outside the panel, with the side it comes from;
  `(WEAK)`, said faintly, in smaller type; `(BURST)`, shouted.
- **A sound where it happens**: `SFX:` with the sound on the line under it, its size in the
  parenthetical, `SFX (small):`.

`examples/gallery/68-a-letterers-script.script` is a page of one:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=68-a-letterers-script.script).

## Written like a screenplay

A writer coming from film writes a cue as a screenplay does, a name in capitals alone on its line
with an extension after it, and Scenet reads the extensions it can letter:

- **`(V.O.)`**, or `(VOICE OVER)`, is a voice over: a spoken caption by the speaker.
  `CAPTION (V.O.)` is one nobody is named for.
- **`(O.S.)`**, and the older `(O.C.)`, is somebody heard from off screen, here off panel, from
  the side the parenthetical names: `KEEPER (O.S., left)`.
- **`(CONT'D)`**, `(beat)` and any word Scenet does not letter by is a note for the artist.

Two habits change. A screenplay puts a parenthetical such as `(whispering)` on the line under
the cue; in a comic script that line is what is said, so the parenthetical goes on the cue's
line. And a slugline in capitals alone on its line looks like a cue, so write the panel's
description after it on the same line: `INT. LIGHTHOUSE - NIGHT. Maya by the dead lamp.`

`examples/gallery/67-written-like-a-screenplay.script` is one, whose last panel recasts the
scene with `@cast` and `@staging`:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=67-written-like-a-screenplay.script).

## Pages

**Each PAGE heading is a page**, and the panels under it are laid out on it, as a scene's
[`pages:`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/page.html#page-and-pages) would lay them out. Dark Horse leaves "exact
panel layout" to the artist, and here the compiler is the artist, so a page's panels go into tiers
by a fixed rule, in reading order:

| Panels | Tiers, top to bottom |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1, 1 |
| 3 | 1, 1, 1 |
| 4 | 2, 2 |
| 5 | 2, 1, 2 |
| 6 | 2, 2, 2 |
| 7 | 2, 3, 2 |
| 8 | 3, 2, 3 |
| 9 | 3, 3, 3 |
| more | rows of three, the extra panels in the earlier tiers: 10 is 3, 3, 2, 2 |

Three tiers is the most up to nine panels, because a page's lettering height assumes three; an odd
panel takes a tier of its own in the middle, where a beat sits best.

**Say otherwise with `@tiers:`**, written right after the PAGE heading and before its first panel:

*Part of a comic script:*

```scenet-script
PAGE TWO
@tiers: 1 2

PANEL 1
...
```

That page's first panel takes the top tier alone, and the next two share the one under it. The
counts must add up to the page's panels; when they do not, or `@tiers:` is written anywhere else,
it is a `page-layout` error at its line. Anything finer — a panel twice as wide, a tier taller than
the rest, columns, insets, slants, a panel that bleeds past the trim — is a scene's `pages:`; see
[Compose a page](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/howto/compose_a_page.html).

**The front matter's `page:` sets the format** every page shares: its size, margin, gutters and
bleed.
A script has no `pages:` key — its pages are its PAGE headings — so writing one is an error.

- **A panel on a page is compiled at the size of its frame**, and every panel on it letters at one
  size, as on any page. The front matter's `panel: {size: ...}` still sizes panels that are on no
  page.
- **Panels before the first PAGE heading are on no page.** They compile on their own, as every
  panel of a script without PAGE headings does.
- **Page files are numbered by position**: `scenet build story.script` writes the first page to
  `story.page-1.svg` whatever its heading says, so an excerpt that starts at `PAGE SEVEN` still
  writes `page-1`. Each panel is written on its own as well, as before.

## A manga, right to left

`direction: rtl` in the front matter makes the whole script read from the top right, as a manga
is read: the panels of each page, and the balloons of each panel. Nothing is mirrored. A
character written at `right_third` stands on the right; only what reading decides follows the
direction, as [`direction`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/direction.html#direction) explains.

*Part of a manga script:*

```scenet-script
---
direction: rtl
page: {size: [1280, 1820], margin: 64, gutter: 24, tier_gutter: 36}
---

PAGE ONE (splash)
```

`(splash)` is a note for the artist, not a count. A manga script numbers each page's panels from
1 again, which names them by page, `2-1` to `2-4`, and `@over: 1` on page two is panel `2-1`.

`examples/gallery/64-a-manga-script.script` is two pages of one, the first in colour:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=64-a-manga-script.script).

## French scripts

A Franco-Belgian script is read in its own words. The vocabulary is the
[Cité internationale de la bande dessinée](https://www.citebd.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/lexique_bd.pdf)'s:

| French | Means |
|---|---|
| `PLANCHE 1 (six cases)` | A page, and its count — `cases` or `vignettes`, in digits or words to *vingt* |
| `CASE 2`, `VIGNETTE 2`, `Case 2 : La plage.` | A panel. Followed by a number only: `CASE` alone is a word, and a cue |
| `RÉCITATIF :`, `CARTOUCHE :`, `NARRATIF :` | A caption, exactly as `CAPTION:` — its kind in the parenthetical, `/NAME` for speech |
| `ONOMATOPÉE : FLOP` | A sound effect, as `SFX:` |
| `LÉA : « Bonjour. »` | A cue and its line. The space before the colon may be a no-break space, and the guillemets are taken off |
| `(pensée)`, `(off)`, `(hors champ)` | A thought balloon; off-panel speech |
| `(murmure)`, `(chuchoté)`; `(cri)`, `(crié)` | A whisper; a shout |
| `(à voix basse)` | Small type, as `(small)` |

*Récitatif*, *cartouche* and *narratif* all name the caption box itself (Cité; Alloprof's
"cartouche (ou récitatif)"; the BnF), which is why they are aliases of `CAPTION` rather than a kind
of their own: the parenthetical says what the box is doing, `CARTOUCHE (monologue)` for a
character's thoughts.

The delivery words are the ones a source defines. The BnF's sheet on balloons draws a dotted
outline for a character who *murmure* — *chuchoter* is to murmur, in Larousse — capitals and
bold for one who *crie*, and smaller type for one who *parle bas*. Any other word, `(hurlé)` say,
stays a note to the artist, as an English one does.

`examples/gallery/33-planche.script` is a planche written in French:
[open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=33-planche.script).

### Shots and angles in French

**Shots and angles may be written in French**, in a comic script's `@shot:` and `@angle:` only — the
YAML language and its schema stay in English. Case, accents, apostrophes and hyphens do not matter,
and the usual abbreviations are read: `GP`, `P.A.`. The *échelle des plans* maps rung for rung onto
[the shot ladder](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/shot_types.html):

| French | Abbreviation | Cuts | `shot` |
|---|---|---|---|
| plan d'ensemble | PE | the setting, figures small | `long_shot` |
| plan moyen | PM | head to foot | `full_shot` |
| plan américain | PA | mid-thigh | `cowboy` |
| plan rapproché taille, plan mi-moyen | PRT, PMM | the waist | `medium_shot` |
| plan rapproché poitrine, plan rapproché | PRP, PR | the chest | `medium_close_up` |
| plan rapproché épaule, plan épaule | | the shoulders | `close_up` |
| gros plan | GP | the face | `big_close_up` |
| très gros plan | TGP | a detail | `extreme_close_up` |

*Gros plan* is `big_close_up` because the French sources put its cut above the shoulders, at the
face: the BnF's *Créer une BD* ("coupé souvent au-dessus des épaules… s'attache au visage"), the
Lyon academy's sheet (at the neck), and French Wikipedia's ladder, which has its own
*plan rapproché épaule* between *plan rapproché* and *gros plan*. Quebec's OQLF defines *gros plan*
at the shoulders instead; writing `plan rapproché épaule` gets that framing. *Plan général* and
*plan italien* have no rung of their own, and `medium_full` no French name; none is invented. The
angles are *plongée* (`high`), *contre-plongée* (`low`) and *angle normal* (`eye_level`).

Two planches in the gallery walk the ladder from the farthest shot to the nearest:
`examples/gallery/65-french-shots-abbreviated.script` in abbreviations, from PE to TGP
([open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=65-french-shots-abbreviated.script)),
and `examples/gallery/66-french-shots-in-full.script` vignette by vignette, every name in full
([open it in the playground](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/playground/#example=66-french-shots-in-full.script)).
The nearest shots letter nothing: the head fills the panel, and no balloon may cover a face.

## Off-panel speech

Dark Horse writes `CHARACTER (OP):` for a character "speaking from off-panel"; Blambot writes
`(OFF)`, and screenplays `(O.S.)` or the older `(O.C.)`. All four mean the same here: the line is
spoken by somebody who is not drawn, and the balloon's tail ends on the frame, on their side —
see [off-panel speech](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/script.html#sayoff_panel).

Off panel means in the scene but out of the frame, and the front matter is the scene's cast. So
`ALICE (OP)` leaves Alice out of **that panel**: out of its cast, and out of every staging relation
that names her — `ALICE left_of BOB` does not apply there, and a `dropped-relation` note says
so. All but one: `BOB looking_at ALICE` still holds, and Bob turns toward the side she is heard
from. Her tail ends on the side she was written to stand on, `at: left_third` being the left, unless
the cue names one: `ALICE (OP, right)`. Somebody never cast — `PHONE (OP)` — is heard just the
same, from the side nearer the balloon.

A panel whose own `@cast:` draws her, or in which she speaks both on and off panel, is
`off-panel-speaker`. A panel `@over:` hers does not inherit her absence: it is worked out from each
panel's own lines.

To leave somebody out of a panel who says nothing in it, write `@cast: {BOB: null}` there. As in
YAML, the relations that name him go with him, each with a `dropped-relation` note. Written for
somebody who then speaks `(OP)`, it says the same as the cue alone.

## One panel over another

Consecutive panels share nearly everything — the place, the weather, who stands where — and
restating it is where continuity errors get in. `@over:` writes a panel as a change to another,
exactly as [`over:`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/howto/compile_a_sequence.html) does in a YAML scene:

*Part of a comic script:*

```scenet-script
PANEL 1
@shot: full_shot
@setting: {place: docks, weather: rain}

PANEL 2
@over: 1
@shot: close_up
```

Panel 2 inherits panel 1's directives and replaces its shot. It never inherits dialogue: each
panel's lines are its own. A label is looked up on the same page first, so `@over: 1` on page two
is panel `2-1`, and then as a panel's whole name, `1-3`. It may name a panel further down. A panel
that does not exist, a cycle, or a panel over itself is one `composition` finding, at the `@over:`
line.

## Prose is never interpreted

"Alice and Bob face each other on a rainy street corner" is not parsed, not
natural-language-processed, and does not affect the output in any way. It is kept because
a script is a document people read, and stripping the description would make the file
worse for its primary audience.

If you want the rain, say so with a directive: `@setting: {weather: rain}` draws it. The
description beside it is never read by the compiler.

It is read by people, though, and not only the artist: a panel's prose is its
[`description`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/description.html#description), what accessible output reads to somebody
who cannot see the panel. Its lines become one paragraph, and Markdown's markers round a word
(`**Alice**`, `_up_`) are taken off. **Everything** the prose says is read — a note to the artist,
`NOTE: redraw the rain.`, included — so when the reader should hear something else, write it as a
directive, which is kept exactly as written and wins over the prose:

*Part of a comic script:*

```scenet-script
PANEL 1
@description: Alice waits on a corner in the rain.
NOTE: redraw the rain, heavier.
```

A panel drawn `@over:` another does not inherit its prose: it is a different picture. A description
in the front matter is refused, since every panel would inherit it. A line of prose holding a
character an SVG cannot hold is reported at that line.

## Front matter

A script is dialogue and camera direction. It has no way to say who `ALICE` *is*, which
puppet she uses, or where she stands. That comes from a YAML preamble between `---`
fences:

*Part of examples/gallery/13-comic-script.script:*

```scenet-script
---
panel:
  size: [900, 700]
cast:
  ALICE: {reference: alice, pose: pointing,     at: left_third}
  BOB:   {reference: bob,   pose: arms_crossed, at: right_third, facing: left}
staging:
  - ALICE left_of BOB
  - ALICE looking_at BOB
  - ALICE ground_shared_with BOB
---

PAGE ONE

PANEL 1
...
```

Everything in the front matter is a default every panel inherits — exactly the same
mechanism as [shared defaults in a sequence](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/howto/compile_a_sequence.html#shared-defaults) — and so a
`description`, which says what one panel shows, is refused there.

`direction: rtl` there makes the whole script read from the top right, as a manga does; see
[`direction`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/direction.html#direction). It is the script's, never one panel's, so
`@direction:` under a PANEL heading is refused.

Note the actor ids are written in caps here, to match the speaker cues. That is a
convention, not a requirement; the ids simply have to agree.

## From Python

```python
from scenet import parse_script

panels = parse_script("""---
cast:
  ALICE: {reference: alice}
---

PANEL 1
@shot: close_up
A quiet room.

ALICE
Is anyone there?

PANEL 2
ALICE (whisper)
Anyone?
""")

# Panels are named by the number in their heading.
assert list(panels) == ["1", "2"]
assert panels["1"].camera.shot.value == "close_up"
assert panels["1"].script[0].text == "Is anyone there?"

# The prose line is interpreted nowhere: it is the panel's description, as written.
assert panels["2"].script[0].kind.value == "whisper"
```

Panel names come straight from the heading, so `PANEL 1` becomes `"1"`. The CLI uses
them as filename suffixes: `umbrella.script` compiles to `umbrella.1.svg`,
`umbrella.2.svg`.

`parse_script` gives you IR;
`load_script` reads a file; and
`compile_document` dispatches on the `.script`
extension so you do not have to care.

## The front matter is not optional in practice

A script with no cast will not parse at all. Validation is total, so a speaker cue naming
somebody who is not in the cast is an error at parse time rather than a blank balloon
discovered later:

```python
from scenet import ScriptSyntaxError, parse_script

try:
    parse_script("PANEL 1" + chr(10) + "ALICE" + chr(10) + "Hello.")
except ScriptSyntaxError as exc:
    assert "unknown actor" in str(exc)
    assert "ALICE" in str(exc)
```

That is the first error you will hit when adapting an existing script: every speaker cue
needs a matching entry in the front-matter cast.

## Both frontends produce the same IR

This is the point of the whole arrangement. `script_front` computes no coordinates and
knows nothing about geometry; it produces the same
`PanelIR` the YAML frontend does, and everything downstream is
unaware that a second syntax exists.

Adding a third syntax means adding a parser and one line in the extension table. Nothing
else changes.

<!-- scenet-spec:part=characters -->
# Characters

The puppets shipped with Scenet. A cast member's `reference` names one of these, and its `pose` and `expression` must be names that puppet declares. `pose` defaults to `standing_neutral` and `expression` to `neutral`.

| Puppet | Heads tall | Poses | Expressions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `alice` | 7.5 | `arms_crossed`, `hands_on_hips`, `pointing`, `standing_neutral` | `angry`, `bored`, `coy`, `happy`, `laughing`, `neutral`, `sad`, `scared`, `shouting`, `surprise` |
| `bob` | 7.5 | `arms_crossed`, `hands_on_hips`, `pointing`, `standing_neutral` | `angry`, `bored`, `coy`, `happy`, `laughing`, `neutral`, `sad`, `scared`, `shouting`, `surprise` |

One puppet may appear several times in a panel under different actor ids.

## A puppet of your own

A `*.puppet.yaml` file beside the document is a puppet of its own, and a cast member names it by its path, relative to the folder the document is in, as a font or a picture is named: `reference: puppets/pip.puppet.yaml`. A reference that ends in `.puppet.yaml` is a file; any other is a shipped puppet's name. The file declares its own poses and expressions, and a member names those. Over MCP, send it in `files` by that path, and `list_puppets` given the same `files` lists it with them. A fault in it is `puppet-file`. What a puppet file holds is in [the asset contract](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/asset_contract.html) and [Add your own character](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/howto/add_your_own_character.html); the gallery's `69-a-puppet-of-your-own.scene.yaml` casts one, printed after it.

## Figures a picture draws

A cast member may instead be `figure: <name>`: somebody a supplied picture (`setting.image`) already draws. No tool lists them, because they are not Scenet's: the names are those the picture's artwork contract declares, in the `*.art.yaml` beside it and named after it (`art/p01.png` has `art/p01.art.yaml`). Over MCP, send the contract in `files` with the picture. A figure takes no `pose`, `expression`, `marks`, `at` or `facing`, no staging names it, and a panel whose cast is all figures has no `camera`; a cast does not mix figures and puppets. See [the artwork contract](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/asset_contract.html#artwork-contracts) and the gallery's `35-figures.scene.yaml`.

<!-- scenet-spec:part=diagnostics -->
# Diagnostics

Everything `scenet check` reports and every note the compiler gives, each with an entry: what
it says, why it happens, how to fix it, the keys that can give it and the release it was
first given in -- then a document that gives it, what the command line prints of that
document, and the same document fixed. Every document on this page is checked by the test
suite: the first of each pair gives exactly that diagnostic, and its fixed twin gives
nothing at all.

The ids are stable across releases. A report prefixes a rule's id with `scenet/`, as
`scenet/unknown-key`; SARIF links each rule here, from its `helpUri`. A compile note's name is
what a gallery example's `notes:` declares it by. The documents name pictures, fonts and a
puppet the gallery has beside it, which the playground has beside every document it opens.

## At a glance

| Id | Level | Says |
|---|---|---|
| [`artwork-contract`](#artwork-contract) | error | A picture's artwork contract cannot be read |
| [`balloon-placement`](#balloon-placement) | error | A balloon or caption has no legal position |
| [`caption-speaker`](#caption-speaker) | error | A caption that is not `spoken` names a speaker |
| [`composition`](#composition) | error | An `over:` chain cannot be resolved |
| [`conflicting-cast`](#conflicting-cast) | error | A cast member is a puppet and a figure, or a cast mixes the two |
| [`conflicting-setting`](#conflicting-setting) | error | A setting says what is behind the cast twice |
| [`duplicate-key`](#duplicate-key) | error | A key is written twice in one mapping |
| [`duplicate-panel`](#duplicate-panel) | error | Two panels in a comic script have the same name |
| [`figure-staging`](#figure-staging) | error | Staging or a camera for figures a picture draws |
| [`font-file`](#font-file) | error | A declared font file cannot be read |
| [`image-file`](#image-file) | error | A supplied picture cannot be read |
| [`internal`](#internal) | error | The compiler failed in a way it does not have a rule for |
| [`invalid-field`](#invalid-field) | error | A field has the wrong shape or value |
| [`layout`](#layout) | error | No layout satisfies the panel's constraints |
| [`missing-field`](#missing-field) | error | A required field is missing |
| [`not-a-mapping`](#not-a-mapping) | error | The document is not a mapping |
| [`off-panel-speaker`](#off-panel-speaker) | error | A line is spoken from off panel by somebody drawn in the panel |
| [`ordering-cycle`](#ordering-cycle) | error | Horizontal ordering contains a cycle |
| [`page-layout`](#page-layout) | error | A page cannot lay out what it says |
| [`panel-direction`](#panel-direction) | error | A panel names a reading direction of its own |
| [`panel-geometry`](#panel-geometry) | error | The panel has no usable area |
| [`puppet-file`](#puppet-file) | error | A puppet file a cast member names cannot be read |
| [`reflexive-relation`](#reflexive-relation) | error | A relation relates an actor to itself |
| [`sfx-placement`](#sfx-placement) | error | A sound effect has no legal position |
| [`syntax`](#syntax) | error | The document is not valid YAML |
| [`unbalanced-emphasis`](#unbalanced-emphasis) | error | Emphasis opened with an underscore is never closed |
| [`unknown-actor`](#unknown-actor) | error | Reference to an actor that is not in the cast |
| [`unknown-expression`](#unknown-expression) | error | Reference to an expression the character does not have |
| [`unknown-figure`](#unknown-figure) | error | A figure the panel's picture does not draw |
| [`unknown-key`](#unknown-key) | error | Unknown key |
| [`unknown-place`](#unknown-place) | error | Reference to a place the library does not have |
| [`unknown-pose`](#unknown-pose) | error | Reference to a pose the character does not have |
| [`unknown-puppet`](#unknown-puppet) | error | Reference to a character the library does not contain |
| [`dropped-relation`](#dropped-relation) | note | A shared staging relation does not apply in a panel its actor is left out of |
| [`looks-like-dialogue`](#looks-like-dialogue) | note | A line in a comic script is set like dialogue but is not read as dialogue |
| [`panel-count`](#panel-count) | note | A comic script's PAGE heading states a count its panels do not match |
| [`word-limit`](#word-limit) | note | A balloon, caption or panel holds more words than a letterer fits well |
| [`bold-italic-stand-in`](#bold-italic-stand-in) | note | No bold italic face is named, so another face stands in for it |
| [`camera-retreated`](#camera-retreated) | note | The camera stepped back so the cast would fit across the panel |
| [`cropped-marks`](#cropped-marks) | note | A character's marks run off the panel at this framing |
| [`cropped-mouth`](#cropped-mouth) | note | A speaking figure's mouth is cropped out of the panel by the picture's fit |
| [`curved-tail`](#curved-tail) | note | A balloon's tail bends around a face |
| [`inset-covers-face`](#inset-covers-face) | note | An inset is drawn over a face |
| [`italic-stand-in`](#italic-stand-in) | note | No italic face is named, so the regular face stands in for it |
| [`slant-cuts-face`](#slant-cuts-face) | note | A slanted gutter cuts across a face |

## Errors

A contradiction the compiler cannot build past. `scenet check` reports it and fails, and `scenet build` stops on the first it meets, exit status 1.

### `artwork-contract`

| | |
|---|---|
| Level | error |
| Says | A picture's artwork contract cannot be read |
| Keys | Every key of [an artwork contract](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/artwork.html); and [`cast.<id>.figure`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/cast.html#castidfigure), [`setting.image`](https://creatoan.github.io/scenet/reference/language/setting.html#settingimage) |
| Since | 0.12 |

**Why it happens.** A panel that casts a figure a supplied picture draws reads the picture's artwork contract, beside it and named after it: `art/p01.png` has its contract at `art/p01.art.yaml`. It must be there, and be YAML holding the picture's `size`, its `figures` and its `keep_out` regions, in the picture's own pixels. The size must be the picture's, every point must lie on the picture, and every region must be a simple polygon. A fault inside the contract is reported in it, when the document was checked as a file.

**How to fix it.** Put the contract beside its picture with the picture's name, measure it on this picture, and check it against `scenet schema --artwork`. The debug overlay (`scenet build --debug`) draws what it declares over the panel.

Checked as `artwork-contract.panel.yaml`:

```yaml
# The street has no artwork contract beside it, so nobody can say where its figures are.
cast: {ana: {figure: ana}}
setting: {image: art/street.png}
```

`scenet check artwork-contract.panel.yaml` says:

```text
artwork-contract.panel.yaml:3:18: artwork-contract: artwork contract file 'art/street.art.yaml' was not found beside the document
```

Fixed:

